newsitem.title: UK: Communist nostalgia, rightist violence mark May Day.
newsitem.headline: Communist nostalgia, rightist violence mark May Day.

text.p: From waves of nostalgia for the Soviet past in Ukraine to violent outbursts by political extremists in northern Germany and ancient fertility dances in rural England, May Day celebrations took many forms on Thursday.

In a display of spring optimism, some 500 left-wing demonstrators marched through the city centre of Bucharest, the Romanian capital, demanding free health care, an end to unemployment and the scrapping of recent price rises.

Nostalgia came to the fore in Ukraine and Belarus, where thousands of people paraded through the streets waving red flags bearing the hammer and sickle of the Soviet Union to which they both belonged until its collapse in 1991. In Minsk, the Belarus capital, marchers held aloft portraits of Soviet founding father Vladimir Lenin, dictator Josef Stalin and the authoritarian Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko.
In Russia itself, tens of thousands marched past the Kremlin walls, pouring forth complaints about economic hardship -- but also downing ample quantities of celebratory vodka.
An estimated 25,000 communist supporters were among them, carrying red flags and slogans demanding the removal of President Boris Yeltsin.

In some cities, the traditional workers' holiday was marred by clashes between demonstrators and police. In the north German town of Muenden, hundreds of neo-Nazis and dozens of left-wing extremists smashed windows and rampaged through the streets after police broke up an illegal right-wing rally.
More than 100,000 Germans joined rallies across the country, protesting against record unemployment and the accompanying rise in right-wing extremism.

Tens of thousands of Turks marched in Istanbul, among them leftist demonstrators accusing the Islamist-led government of links to a security scandal. "Money for health, not for the gangs," and "Money for education, not for the gangs," chanted the marchers, some of whom clashed with police trying to stop them marching towards the city centre.

Politics was to the fore in Paris, where far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and his National Front launched their drive for a toehold in parliament in the May-June elections with a vitriolic speech to some 9,000 supporters. Le Pen accused President Jacques Chirac of ignoring immigration and high unemployment and trying to jettison France's national identity, and urged the cheering crowd to throw him out. A May Day march in the Polish capital Warsaw produced an unlikely political twist when the ruling ex-communists produced a long red banner proclaiming "Good luck, Tony Blair," and a large portrait of Blair, whose opposition Labour Party is widely expected to win British parliamentary elections taking place today.
Blair has used his leadership of the party to modernise it, weakening traditional ties with the unions and positioning it close to the centre of the British political stage.

In Britain itself, May 1 is not a public holiday and is marked not by workers' marches but by traditions such as dancing round the May Pole on village greens, remnants of an ancient fertility rite, and displays by local troupes of folk dancers.
A striking contrast to such bucolic delights was the May Day demonstration by some 200 Palestinians at a Jewish settlement construction site in Arab East Jerusalem.

The protesters called on Israel to stop the bulldozers at Jabal Abu Ghneim where the Jewish state is building 6,500 homes for Jews. Palestinians claim East Jerusalem as the capital of their future state.
